candidates.source_name: Cyril of Alexandria / Commentary on Luke
candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CVII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's 'joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth, more than over ninety and nine just persons, which need no repentance' (Lk 15:7), Cyril reads the more-joy-over-one-sinner-repenting as the canonical Lukan anchor of the heaven-rejoices doctrine: the conversion of a single soul is not a private-individual event but a cosmic-angelic celebration. The 'more joy' is not comparative-quantitative but pastoral-emphatic — Cyril preserves the divine preference for the rescuing-pattern. Tewahedo missionary-spirituality cites Lk 15:7 + Lk 15:10 (joy in the presence of the angels) as the canonical doubled-witness of the doctrine that the angelic host participates joyfully in each conversion; the Tewahedo evangelistic-prayer tradition invokes the angels' rejoicing.

candidates.source_name: Cyril of Alexandria / Commentary on Luke
candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CVIII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the parable of the lost coin — 'Either what woman having ten pieces of silver, if she lose one piece, doth not light a candle, and sweep the house, and seek diligently till she find it?' (Lk 15:8) — Cyril reads the maternal-housekeeping-image as the canonical Lukan anchor of a doctrine that complements the shepherd-image (Lk 15:4) and the father-image (Lk 15:11): God seeks the lost in three iconic ways — shepherd seeking on the hills, woman seeking in the house, father waiting at the door. The triple-image is Trinitarian-iconic-pedagogy. Tewahedo Trinitarian-iconography cites Lk 15:4-32 as the canonical Lukan iconographic triple-pattern of the Father-Son-Spirit's-shared-search-for-the-lost.

candidates.source_name: Cyril of Alexandria / Commentary on Luke
candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CIX (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the parable's opening 'A certain man had two sons' (Lk 15:11), Cyril reads the two-sons frame as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the parable's THIRD pivot (after shepherd + housekeeper) gives the Father his speaking-part: the father whose first speech is the silent embrace at 15:20, whose second speech is the celebration-command, whose third is the explanation to the elder brother. The full-pericope (Lk 15:11-32) is Christ's most-extended-character-development parable; the father's character is most-fully-disclosed. Tewahedo pastoral theology cites Lk 15:11-32 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of the Father's threefold-speech-of-mercy — the priest who absolves speaks as the father in the parable speaks.

candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CVII (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

'When he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him' — Cyril treats the Father's running as the canonical signature of the Lukan parable: the divine compassion does not wait for the sinner to arrive but goes out to meet him while he is still far. The first robe, the ring, and the shoes are the baptismal restoration of dignity. Tewahedo penitential theology cites Lk 15:20-22 as the principal canonical anchor of God-runs-to-meet-the-returning-sinner imagery.

candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CX (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Rom 6:4.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the father's final words to the elder brother 'It was meet that we should make merry, and be glad: for this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found' (Lk 15:32), Cyril reads the doubled-formula (dead-and-alive + lost-and-found) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of conversion-as-resurrection: the prodigal's return is not merely moral-improvement but a passage from death to life. The same doubled-formula echoes Christian baptism (Rom 6:4 — dead with Christ, alive in Christ). Tewahedo baptismal-and-penance theology cites Lk 15:32 + Rom 6:4 as the canonical doubled-witness that every conversion is a participation in the death-and-resurrection of Christ; the Tewahedo penance-rite preserves the alive-again grammar in its absolution formula.
